chapters.title: Start here: keep what you already have
chapters.brief: Why a parent going through divorce or a custody case keeps dated copies and notes: memory fades under stress, and a lawyer, mediator or court self-help center can only work with what the parent can show them. The scope rule: keep copies of papers and messages you already have or that were sent to you, and notes you write yourself. Never go into a spouse's phone, email or accounts, never record anyone in secret, and never move or hide money; ask a lawyer what is allowed where you live. End with what the rest of the book gives them: a checklist, logs and the official court pages for their state.

chapters.title: How to keep a co-parenting log
chapters.brief: How to write log entries that stay useful: the same day, date and time first, what was planned and what actually happened, facts not feelings, the child's words in quotes only if the parent heard them directly, no guesses about the other parent's motives, short entries, corrections added as a new dated line instead of erasing. A good entry and a weak entry side by side, as an invented example with no names (use 'the other parent' and 'our child'). Keep the log in one place: a notebook, the printable log, or an app.

chapters.title: Saving messages, photos and screenshots from your own phone
chapters.brief: Practical steps for keeping copies of messages that were sent to the reader: screenshot the whole conversation with the date visible, keep the original messages on the phone too, export or email copies to themself where the app allows it, note in the messages log where each copy is saved, keep photos with their original dates, keep a backup in a second place. Never edit or crop a copy in a way that changes what it says. Only the reader's own phone and accounts.

chapters.title: Gathering the papers before you meet a lawyer or mediator
chapters.brief: Walk through the seven checklist groups in plain words (bank, retirement and debt statements; pay stubs and tax returns; household bills and expenses; home, car and property papers; agreements and court papers you already have; messages sent to you; the co-parenting log) and what a copy of each usually looks like. Suggest making one folder per group and one list of what is in it, and bringing copies, never the only original. Say plainly that what is needed varies by state and by case, and the lawyer or the court's self-help center says what matters for theirs.

chapters.title: Writing to the other parent when things are tense
chapters.brief: How to keep messages to the other parent short, polite and about the child and the schedule, because anything written may be read later by others. Answer the question asked, confirm times and places in writing, avoid sarcasm, threats and long arguments, wait before replying when angry, and use one channel when possible. No legal advice and no claims about what courts think.

chapters.title: Where to get help
chapters.brief: Point to the kinds of help that exist without promising any: the court's own self-help center or family law facilitator (most state court websites have one; the state pages at the back of this book link to official ones), legal aid organizations for people with lower incomes, the local bar association's lawyer referral service, and mediators. If anyone is in danger, call 911; protective orders are covered for each state at the back. Remind the reader that this book is not legal advice and that rules differ by state.

series_books.author: Reid Calloway
series_books.title: Parallel Parenting
series_books.subtitle: A Simple Record Book for High-Conflict Co-Parents: Calm Message Rules, Handoff Logs and One Place for Every Paper
series_books.description:
When every message turns into an argument, co-parenting the usual way stops working. Parallel parenting is the quieter alternative: each parent runs their own time, contact shrinks to the logistics, and everything is written down.

This short record book shows you how to set that up and keep it going, without becoming a full-time investigator of the other parent.

Inside:
- What parallel parenting is, and when it helps
- Written rules for one channel, short replies and set response times, with the BIFF reply shape and invented examples
- Handoffs without a scene: places, timing and what to note afterwards
- How to write log entries that stay useful: dated, factual, boring
- Keeping your child out of the middle
- Fill-in logs for handoffs, messages, schedule changes, expenses and reply drafts
- A checklist of the papers to keep in one place, and official sources by state

Every log can also be printed free from the KeepMyProof website.

This book is educational only and is not legal advice. It makes no predictions about any case, and a record you keep is your own account, nothing more. Rules differ by state; ask your court's self-help center or a lawyer.

Published by Spry Labs, the makers of KeepMyProof, a private phone app for keeping these papers in dated folders.

series_books.description:
Something is wrong at your job: comments, threats, being singled out, hours cut after you spoke up. You are told to "document everything", but nobody says how.

This short workbook shows you how to keep a calm, dated record of what happened, using only what you received or wrote yourself, so the people helping you (HR, an agency, a lawyer) can see it clearly.

Inside:
- What the phrase means in everyday words, and what this book can and cannot do
- Same-day incident notes: who, what, where, exact words, with a weak and a good example
- Saving messages and papers you are allowed to keep, and what never to take
- Comparing your own hours with your pay stubs
- Putting a complaint in writing and keeping every reply
- Looking after yourself while it is going on
- Fill-in logs for incidents, pay, complaints and time off, plus official agency sources by state

This book is educational only and is not legal advice. It makes no predictions about any outcome. Deadlines differ by state and agency; check the official sources at the back or ask a lawyer.

series_books.title: Your VA Disability Rating
series_books.subtitle: The Papers to Gather Before You Claim, Appeal or Ask for an Increase, With Logs for Exams, Mail and Buddy Statements
series_books.description:
A VA disability decision is made from paper: service records, medical records, statements and exam notes. Missing papers are one of the most common reasons veterans wait longer or try again.

This short binder walks you through gathering, copying and keeping those papers in order, whether you are filing a first claim, asking for an increase or reviewing a decision. It never predicts a rating.

Inside:
- How a rating is decided, in plain words
- Service papers and records: what to request and how to keep originals safe
- Medical records and getting ready for the exam, including how to describe bad days honestly
- Statements from people who know: who can write one and what it covers
- The review lanes after a decision, and which papers each one needs
- Free, accredited help, and warning signs of people who charge for what is free
- Fill-in logs for appointments, mail, statements and symptoms, plus official sources by state

Not affiliated with the Department of Veterans Affairs. Educational only; not legal or medical advice.

Published by Spry Labs, the makers of KeepMyProof.

series_books.subtitle: A Parent's Record of School Notes, Requests and Follow-Ups, With the Questions to Ask Each Time You Sit Down
series_books.description:
Walking into a school meeting about your child's support can feel like walking into a room where everyone else has the papers. This binder makes sure you have them too.

It explains the difference between a 504 plan and an IEP in plain words, then shows you how to keep your own record: what you asked for, what was agreed, and whether it is actually happening in the classroom.

Inside:
- 504 plan or IEP: the difference in plain words
- Setting up the binder in one afternoon
- Asking in writing, and keeping every reply
- Before, during and after the meeting, with questions to bring
- A weekly check to see whether the plan is followed
- Where parents get free help
- Fill-in pages for meeting notes, written requests, school messages and weekly checks, plus official parent centers by state

The paperback is 8.5 x 11 inches so pages can be hole-punched and filed with school papers.

Educational only; not legal advice and no advice about which services a child should get.

series_books.title: What to Do When Someone Dies
series_books.subtitle: The Executor's Checklist for the First Week, the First Month and Settling the Estate, With Space for Every Account
series_books.description:
When someone close to you dies, the paperwork arrives while you are still in shock. This checklist book takes it one step at a time: what really needs doing in the first week, what can wait a month, and how to keep track of every account until the estate is settled.

Inside:
- You do not have to do it all today: what the first days really need
- The first week: death certificates, securing the home, mail, telling people
- The first month: the will, whether probate may be needed, benefits, employers and pensions
- Finding every account and property, including family land passed down without a will
- Bills and debts, and why not to pay from your own pocket before asking
- Closing the estate and keeping the records afterwards
- Looking after yourself while you do it
- Fill-in pages for tasks, accounts, calls and money in and out, plus official probate sources by state

The paperback is 8.5 x 11 inches, with room to write.

Educational only; not legal or tax advice. The probate court or a lawyer says what applies to your estate.
